en: They called his customs Kalmyk.
The offspring of the Blood-Drinker
He was pure from birth,
A hero like a holy seer.
Your father who went to the other world—
He was a hero equal to him in spirit.
When Almambet came to Beijing,
Clouds stirred in the sky.
Your holy father, the lion—
He was his friend on twelve occasions.
Stars stirred in the heavens.
Your lion father, the great beast—
He was his friend on six occasions.
I tell of my Almam's valor;
Listen mindfully, little one!
When he scattered the unbelievers' livestock,
When he opened the way of Islam,
The countless cattle the Chinese had gathered in taxes,
Ten thousand head belonging to the treasury,
When he drove them toward this side,
The khans of the populous Chinese,
When their khan came surging,
The massed Chinese and many Manchus,
When they all came surging,
My perfect, fierce-maned Almam
Girded his waist with a leather belt.
Against seven multitudes of Kara-Chinese,
He went in alone and attacked.
My precious, renowned Almam
Speared warriors on the downward slope,
Pierced many alike, one after another.
When he struck, spears shattered.
Saying, 'He has gone over to the Kyrgyz,'
The unbelievers' khan Kongurbay
Wept, unable to find a remedy.
Who was it that speared those warriors?
My precious lion Almam speared them,
But the renown went to Manas.
Do not ask of my Alake:
When my Almam settled in Talas,
Your exceptional father Manas
Through her thoughtful arrangements,
His countless treasures and possessions
He filled with yellow gold.
He made the yurt's side-felts greasy,
Made everyone he met rich.
He hid the livestock enclosure in dust.
Alas, when my Almam came,
He raised the khan's realm above all others.
That is what is known.
Esen Khan's Burulcha
Was my Alake's wife.
Saying this, mighty Bakay,
At the spur where the mountain ends,
At the promontory of the level mountain,
From the dark ridge's rise,
When your uncle Bakay Khan looked,
A torn black yurt stood there.
When he rode farther on,
A black cow with a torn nostril stood there.
The yurt they had pitched—
Its covering had split apart,
Its lattice and roof-poles showed.
Seeing this, mighty Bakay,
His golden-cheeked battle-axe
Propped against his right flank,
Semetey and Bakay Khan
Now raised their voices in lament.
When Bakay Khan raised his voice,
Could the orphan boy stand silent?
Semetey joined in the lament:
"If six great rivers joined,
You were their confluence, my mighty father!
Of a great mountain beyond sight,
You were its spur, my mighty father!
Of a great mountain with lofty passes,
You were its ridge, my mighty father!
Of a bulletproof battle-coat,
You were its breast, my mighty father!
Of the keen blades of black steel,
You were their metal, my mighty father!
Of a valley where meadowsweet grows,
You were its hollow, my mighty father!
Which Manas had tempered—
You were his steel, my mighty father!
Left behind you with a bad name,
With no means to stir,
There is a wretch like the wind.
Bereft of his kin,
Is there a wretch like me?
Strained and hurled vile words.
To gird my waist firmly,
Against Kongurbay in Beijing,
To pursue blood-payment for my father Manas,
Perishable world, may you come to ruin!
Neither Almambet nor Syrgak is here.
The time of my full strength has not come.
To take revenge upon the unbelievers,
To wreak havoc,
Chubak, son of Baltay Khan, is not here.
To Temir Khan's city
I wandered away and returned.
Bereft of mane and tail,
I am like a wild ass;
Bereft of all my legs,
I am like a snake.
You who pledged allegiance to twelve spiritual masters,
My holy father, why did you die?
Bereft of you in death, your household grieves—
Why must it howl and wander?
Humiliation such as this,
If God creates a living soul,
Upon any mortal in the whole world
May He never bring it down!
May God never take away a prince;
May no wife be left behind by a prince.
You never pulled back the smoke-hole cover,
Never ate food left overnight.
Your seat was a golden throne,
You never left your pleasures.
You were the beauty among women,
Burulcha, wife of my father's sworn friend,
You were the daughter of Esen Khan.
In mourning, crying through the night,
When my Almam Khan passed away,
You became a slave to cattleherds.
Mother by sworn kinship, have you come to this?
The prince's young camel,
Fleeing away to Bukhara,
Unable to give his people even his presence—
Have I come to this?
Living through days of hardship,
Mother by sworn kinship, Burulcha,
Have you come to this?
To the khan's city of Bukhara,
After my khan father passed away,
I fled in disgrace.
My precious mother Kanykey,
The beauty among the dark-complexioned,
The radiant one among Muslims,
Her precious quail-like eyes
Shed tears in separate streams;
Her precious currant-like eyes
Shed tears a whip's length long.
Crying out, she entrusted it to me;
Sobbing, she gave me her charge.
The dress of fine white cloth my mother gave—
It would be shameful not to give it to you.
It is her trust for you.
Mother by sworn kinship, Burulcha,
The dress my mother gave,
I offer as a gift; put it on.
My valiant, fiery mother,
Always remember her."
When the orphan gave her the dress,
When the dress reached her hands,
When sorrowful Burulcha put it on,
How could Burulcha restrain herself?
She lamented her former days:
"When my prince was still alive,
My precious hair fell in tresses.
After my prince passed away,
After your sworn friend's soul went to the other world,
My precious head fell prey to plunder.
This world is false;
I stand worn down by its troubles.
For the one child Kulchoro,
I have served a cattleherd.
I wish to die of shame.
That I remain alive, not dead,
Is because Kulchoro is here.
Crying out under torment,
One day the thought came to me to die,
To see the face of Judgment Day.
Killed,
Thinking to die,
For six calves and four yearlings
I had bought a bright dagger.
I grasped it by the hilt,
Drew it from its sheath.
As I aimed it toward my heart,
Almambet, gone to the other world—
As I was about to join him,
Kulchoro, then three years old,
Grabbed at my knife with his little hands,
Clambering, refusing to let go.
Though I meant to die of shame,
In the end I did not die,
Because Kulchoro was here.
'If I should suddenly die,
If I should falter in human weakness,
My long-awaited only child,
Kulchoro would be left helpless,' I thought.
'Abyke, Kobosh, the six scoundrels—
With neither mother nor father at all,
They would make him a slave for life.'
I have seen the world's falsehood;
For him I stayed alive.
My fate was unhappy.
After your Alake passed away,
Perish, world, with your day of taking life!
My share in life's blessings was scant.
The hair at my nape was like grass.
After your Alake passed away,
My ruin exceeded my joy
By many a spear's length.
What I dug was a deep pit;
What I faced was profound sorrow.
I prayed for my only child Kulchoro.
The whip those dogs struck with—
Would God take me merely for lamenting?
Will it ever leave my aching bones?
I still have more to say.
What drove all peace from my mind—
Yesterday, I heard, they beat
The child fate had granted me.
If the moon is veiled in darkness,
That is what the night is like.
If death arrives and a khan dies,
For those left behind him,
That is what life is like.
I have a deep pit dug for me,
I have inescapable sorrow.
To tell you in lament,
My orphan, I have many tales.
When your father's sworn friend lived,
Your poor mother by sworn kinship
Had black hair falling in tresses.
After your father's sworn friend died,
My head has been subject to plunder.
I have endured much humiliation,
I have only a spoonful of blood left.
When I think of it, life is sweet,
But grief weighs down my soul.
A line has been drawn for me.
If I tell you, my orphan,
There are many marvels to recount.
In Beijing, where even the Flood cannot reach,
When they slaughtered without stopping,
The unbelievers, numerous as dust—
When they seized their khan's realm,
Upon the Kara-Chinese and Manchus
They wreaked havoc.
When Beijing with its forty gates—
They subdued its khan blessed by Kydyr,
Not exhausted by feasting till Judgment Day,
The Chinese treasury of red gold—
When the champions entered and scattered it,
Upon the damned Chinese
They inflicted a great slaughter.
They destroyed their mighty men,
And carried off their daughters.
I was the beauty among women,
Of Beijing's Chynchy Khan
I was truly the cherished daughter.
Of Esen Khan, seated on his throne,
